summary: Most reviewers find the Axiom Crave a straight, accurate fairway driver that goes farther than its speed suggests and holds lines well, including on forehands. The main downside is inconsistency: flight changes a lot with plastic, weight and run, and some copies turn over or get flippy quickly.

Most reviewers use the Westside Harp as a very overstable approach disc and driving putter, valued for a reliable fade, forehand use and steadiness in wind. The deep rim gives a grippy feel but is too deep for some. Downsides: little glide and short distance, and some plastics beat in or turn flippy.

Most reviewers praise the Innova Wraith for distance, especially on forehand, and for how it flips and glides once seasoned. The main downside is variation: stability differs a lot between plastics and runs, and many copies beat in quickly and turn flippy. Several owners bag it in a few plastics to cover different stabilities.

Most reviewers use the Kastaplast Berg as a low-glide approach and putting disc, valued for landing and sitting near the target without skipping, and for going straight on forehands. It holds lines and is unbothered by wind. Downsides: it gives little distance or glide, and some find it gets flippier as it beats in.

Most reviewers find the Innova Mako3 a very straight, honest midrange that holds whatever line it is released on, which makes it popular with beginners learning form. The downsides are inconsistency between plastics, weights and copies, and a tendency to turn over as it beats in. Holding lines also makes it unforgiving of release errors for some.

Most reviewers describe the Axiom Hex as a straight, predictable midrange with a low-profile, comfortable grip, often compared to a Buzzz that feels better in the hand, and it handles forehands well. The main downside is that stability varies by plastic and run, from flippy to quite overstable.

Most reviewers rely on the Innova TeeBird3 as a workhorse fairway driver with a straight flight and reliable fade, good on forehand and backhand and in wind. It is often more overstable than expected when new, especially in metal flake and Halo plastics, so some feel it is not a beginner disc until beaten in.

Most reviewers praise the MVP Wave for distance, especially on hyzer flips and turnovers at moderate arm speeds. The main downside is flippiness: it often turns over, light Fission copies especially, and stability varies by plastic, weight and run, with Neutron and Eclipse noticeably steadier.

Reviewers who like the MVP Trail value its easy distance and glide, even at modest arm speeds. The dominant complaint is inconsistency: copies from different runs, weights and plastics range from very overstable to roller-flippy, and many get flippier as they beat in. Light weights in particular tend to turn over.

Most reviewers describe the MVP Detour as an understable midrange that flips up from hyzer and flies straight or drifts right with little fade, with good distance and forehand use through gaps. The main downside is that it can turn over too easily for some, and it is often described as flippier than a Hex.

Most reviewers use the Streamline Pilot mainly as a putting putter, praising its shallow, comfortable feel and a straight, glidey flight that also works for throwing and approaches. Stability depends on plastic, with Electron feeling soft and grippy and Neutron and Proton steadier. A few find it too glidey or understable.

Most reviewers find the MVP Reactor a slightly overstable midrange with a straight flight and dependable fade, torque resistant and especially good on forehands, and many prefer it to a Hex for that. Stability varies by plastic, with Eclipse and glow noticeably beefier. Complaints are few.

Most reviewers like the Latitude 64 Pure as both a putting and throwing putter, praising its shallow, comfortable feel and a flight that holds whatever line it is put on. Plastics differ, with Opto often chosen for throwing and Zero for putting. Complaints are scattered, such as limited glide on longer putts.

Most reviewers describe the MVP Resistor as a very overstable fairway driver, a slower baby Firebird, favored for forehands, utility shots and wind. The main downside is inconsistency between runs and plastics: some copies are extremely beefy and short, while newer runs can fly closer to a Servo.

Most reviewers find the MVP Tesla more overstable than its numbers suggest, flying straight and fading hard like a Firebird or Thunderbird, and it is popular as a forehand driver. The main downside is that many copies are meathooks, especially backhand or at lower arm speeds, though they beat in toward straighter flights.

Most reviewers like the Latitude 64 River for its lots of glide and easy distance, and it suits beginners and slower arms as a controllable driver. The main downsides are that it is understable, turns over with power, and gets flippier as it beats in, with some variation between plastics.

Most reviewers find the Latitude 64 Fuse a very straight, glidey understable midrange that flips up flat with little fade, good for beginners, forehands and tight wooded lines. The main downside is that it turns over easily and gets flippier as it beats in, so some find it too flippy.

Most reviewers find the MVP Volt more overstable than its numbers suggest, a beefy fairway driver with a dependable fade, used for forehands and wind. The main downside is that many copies are very overstable and short, some called meathooks, though several beat in to straighter or turnover flights.

Most reviewers use the Axiom Envy as a throwing putter for straight shots and approaches, praising its accuracy, comfortable grip and surprising distance. The main downside is that flight differs by plastic and wear, from fairly overstable when new to flippy once beaten in.

Most reviewers use the Discraft Zone as an overstable approach disc, especially forehand, valued for a straight line and a dependable fade that makes landing spots predictable. Many call it torque resistant and steady in wind. Complaints are few, mainly stability changing with plastic and beat-in.
